meta.title: Rebuild a live client site as a Next.js and Supabase site
meta.lead: How an existing client website becomes a new Next.js site built from the HGM template, matched section by section against the original. If you remember one thing: the live site is the reference, not your memory — every section is judged against a saved capture of the original, never against what looks about right on screen.
meta.frequency: Every AI website build request in Asana

items.d: Turns an existing client website into a new Next.js site built from the HGM AI website template, hosted on Netlify, with Supabase as the database and the client's property management system as the booking API. The finished site is a faithful copy of the original on its netlify.app address, ready for pre-launch checks.

Making the repository, connecting Netlify, collecting every key the build needs, gathering reference material, writing and executing the plan, matching every page and section to the original, building the forms and pop-up, checking the build works, and taking it through team, account manager and client review to approval.

Everything after client approval belongs to WEB-005: SEO and GEO, accessibility, Lighthouse, BrowserStack, legal pages, the money path, the test booking and the DNS cutover. Analytics and Search Console belong to WEB-003, after launch.

blocks.text: This SOP covers the case where a live website already exists and is being reproduced. Building a site from a Figma design with no live original is a separate SOP, not yet written.

blocks.t: Five standing rules
blocks.d: True on every build.

items.t: The live site is the reference
items.d: Judge every section against a saved capture in Resources/, not against how it looks.
Stop at the property page. The money path is WEB-005's job.

items.t: Secret keys live in two places
items.d: .env.local and the client's 1Password vault. Never in a commit, a prompt or a screenshot.
The site stays on its *.netlify.app address until the WEB-005 cutover.
Every session adds a row to TOKENS.md.

items.t: Access to the hgmwebteam GitHub organisation
items.d: Enough to create a repository from a private template. Ask the template owner if Use this template is not offered.
Netlify is the client's own account, not HGM's. The credentials are on the client's record in hgmportal.com.

items.t: Access to the client's GoHighLevel sub-account
items.d: The site's forms are built there and embedded here. You need the sub-account, not the agency view.
The portal holds the client record: which property management system they are on, and the keys HGM already has.
Client logins and the site's .env.local entry live here. See HGM-SOP-WEB-001.

items.t: VS Code with Claude Code signed in
items.d: Every task in this SOP is done in VS Code with Claude Code. Node and npm installed — HGM-SOP-WEB-002 task 1.1 lists the four tools.

items.t: The URL of the live site
items.d: The site being reproduced. It must still be reachable; once DNS moves at launch it is gone.
The original site's stylesheets and computed styles are where the design tokens come from. Chrome or Firefox, with the Elements and Network panels.
The build request. It carries the client, the deadline and anything the account manager has already agreed.

blocks.d: Pick the right template for the client's booking platform and make the site's own repository from it. Do this once, at the start of a build.

blocks.t: Find out which booking platform the client uses
blocks.d: Open hgmportal.com, find the client's record, and read which property management system they are on.
blocks.expect: You know the client is on Guesty or on Hostaway. Every later choice — template, plan, API keys — follows from this one.

body.t: Do not guess from the old site
body.text: A WordPress site can front any booking platform, and some front more than one. The portal record is the answer. If the portal has no record, ask the account manager named on the Asana task before you start.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — The client's record on hgmportal.com, cropped to the property management system field. Ring the PMS field.

blocks.t: Open the matching template repository
blocks.d: In GitHub, open the hgmwebteam organisation and open ai-website-template-guesty or ai-website-template-hostaway, whichever matches the answer from task 1.1.
blocks.expect: The repository page shows the Private template badge beside its name.

body.caption: The two site templates in the hgmwebteam organisation. Pick the one matching the client's booking platform.

body.t: No template for this booking platform
body.text: If the client is on a platform with no template — Cloudbeds, for example — start from [NEEDS INPUT: the name of the standard AI website template repository in hgmwebteam] or from whichever PMS template is closer, then tell Claude the platform is different in task 6.2. Do not start building against the wrong platform's booking engine.

blocks.t: Create the site's repository from the template
blocks.d: Click Use this template, then Create a new repository. Set the owner to hgmwebteam, name it after the client in lower case with hyphens — for example ridge-and-falls — and set it to Private.
blocks.expect: A new repository exists at github.com/hgmwebteam/<client-name> with the template's files and no commit history from the template.

body.caption: Use this template, at the top right of the template repository.

body.t: Why a template and not a fork
body.text: A fork keeps a link back to the template and carries its history. A template copy starts clean, which is what a client site wants — the template's own history is not this client's history.

blocks.t: Read the template's own documentation before touching anything
blocks.d: In the new repository, read README.md, SETUP.md, NEW-SITE-CHECKLIST.md and UPSTREAM.md. They describe this version of the template, which moves faster than this SOP does.
blocks.expect: You know what the template already ships — booking engine, admin dashboard, checkout, email — so you do not rebuild something that is already there.

body.caption: The template's documentation files, beside PLAN.md and ENV.template in the repository root.

body.t: Where the template and this SOP disagree, the template wins
body.text: The template is the running code. If SETUP.md contradicts a task here, follow SETUP.md, finish the build, then tell the Web & Content Specialist so this document gets fixed rather than quietly ignored.

blocks.text: Phase 2 — Connect the repository to Netlify
blocks.d: Get HGM onto the client's Netlify account, then give the site a real address before any code is written — the address is itself a value the build needs.

blocks.t: Sign in to the client's Netlify account and add HGM to it
blocks.d: Sign in to Netlify with the client's credentials from their record on hgmportal.com. Go to Team settings → Members, invite hgmwebteam@gmail.com (the HGM web team account) and give it the Developer role. Every new client Netlify, Supabase and Resend account gets this invite (tasks 2.1, 4.2 and 4.7), so the team's automations connect with nothing else to set up.
blocks.expect: The HGM web team account can reach the team, create projects, set environment variables and deploy, without being able to change billing or delete the team.

body.t: Developer, not Owner
body.text: Netlify's own guidance is to grant the least access that does the job. Developer covers everything this SOP needs. Owner additionally carries billing and the ability to delete the team, which is not HGM's to hold on a client account. If the client's plan only offers Owner, Collaborator and Billing Admin, choose Collaborator.

body.t: The account is the client's, permanently
body.text: The client pays for and owns the Netlify team. HGM is a member of it. That is what lets the relationship end without the site having to move.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — Netlify Team settings → Members with the invite dialog open and the role list showing. Ring the Developer option.

blocks.t: Import the repository into Netlify
blocks.d: In Netlify, click Add new project, then Import an existing project, then GitHub, then choose hgmwebteam/<client-name>. Accept the build settings the template supplies and click Deploy.
blocks.expect: A Netlify project exists and its first build starts. That build will fail, because no environment variables are set yet. That is expected and is fixed in task 4.11.

body.t: Connect the repository, do not create the site from the command line
body.text: A site created with the Netlify CLI has no Git connection, so nothing rebuilds when anyone pushes. Importing the repository is what makes every later push publish.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — Netlify Import an existing project → GitHub, with the repository list showing. Ring the repository row.

blocks.t: Record the site's address
blocks.d: Copy the project's *.netlify.app address from the Netlify project overview and paste it into the Asana task as a comment.
blocks.expect: The team can reach the build without asking you, and you have the value task 4.5 needs.

body.t: No custom domain in this SOP
body.text: Pointing the client's real domain at this project takes their current site down. The DNS cutover happens at launch, after the client has approved the build — see WEB-005.

blocks.text: Phase 3 — Open the site on your machine
blocks.d: Get your own copy running locally. If this is your first time on this computer, do the machine setup in HGM-SOP-WEB-002 first.

blocks.t: Clone the repository into VS Code
blocks.d: In a new VS Code window, open the Explorer and click Clone Repository, then paste the repository URL from GitHub's Code button.
blocks.expect: VS Code asks where to save it, then asks whether to open it. Open it.

body.t: The long version lives in WEB-002
body.text: HGM-SOP-WEB-002 tasks 1.1 to 1.7 cover installing the four tools, cloning and running npm install, with a screenshot on every click. Follow it the first time; come back here once the repository is open.

body.label: Or ask Claude to clone it
body.text:
Clone https://github.com/hgmwebteam/<client-name>.git into
this folder and open it. Tell me if anything fails.

blocks.t: Install the packages
blocks.d: Paste the prompt into Claude Code.
blocks.expect: Claude reports it finished without an error, and a node_modules folder appears. It takes a few minutes the first time.

body.label: Claude prompt
body.text: Run npm install in this project and tell me if anything fails.

blocks.t: Make your own environment file
blocks.d: In the Explorer, right-click the template's environment example file in the repository root — ENV.template in the current templates — choose Copy, then Paste, and rename the copy to .env.local.
blocks.expect: .env.local sits in the repository root and is greyed out in the Explorer, because .gitignore excludes it. If it is not greyed out, stop and check .gitignore before you put a key in it.

body.caption: Right-click the environment example file and choose Copy. The same menu carries Copy Relative Path, used later when a prompt needs an exact file path.

body.t: Do not put NETLIFY_SITE_ID in .env.local
body.text: Setting it locally flips the site into its deployed-Netlify behaviour while you are on localhost: images start requesting Netlify's image CDN and 404, and the local booking store points at the deployed site's storage. Leave it unset locally and set it on Netlify only.

blocks.t: Start the cost file
blocks.d: Create TOKENS.md in the repository root with one heading and a table — date, session, approximate tokens, cost in Canadian dollars — and commit it.
blocks.expect: Every later session has somewhere to record what it cost. Task 8.1 fills in a row.

body.label: Claude prompt
body.text:
Create TOKENS.md in the repository root with the heading
"# Token spend" and an empty table with the columns Date,
Session, Approx. tokens and Cost (CAD). Commit it with the
message "chore: start token spend log".

blocks.d: Fill in as much of the environment file as you can get today, set the same values on Netlify, and write the result back to 1Password.

blocks.t: Take the keys HGM already holds from the portal
blocks.d: Open hgmportal.com, open the client's record, and copy every key it holds for this client into .env.local, matching each one to the variable name in ENV.template.
blocks.expect: The variables HGM can supply without the client are filled in.

body.t: Some values are the same for every client
body.text: A small number of platform credentials are held once at the agency and reused — the portal record is where you find out which. Never copy one from another client's .env.local; take it from the portal.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — The keys section of the client's record on hgmportal.com, with every value redacted before you send it.

blocks.t: Get into the client's Supabase project and add the web team to it
blocks.d: Sign in to Supabase with the client's credentials from 1Password, open their project, then invite hgmwebteam@gmail.com as a member under Project settings → Members.
blocks.expect: You can reach the project signed in as hgmwebteam@gmail.com, and you stop using the client's login from this point on.

body.t: The client owns this project
body.text: The Supabase project is created in the client's own account, not HGM's. Adding the web team account as a member is what lets the team's automations connect, and it survives a password change on their side.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — Supabase Project settings → Members with the invite dialog open. Ring the Invite button.

blocks.t: Open the project's API keys
blocks.d: In the Supabase project, go to Project settings → API Keys, then click the Legacy anon, service_role API keys tab.
blocks.expect: The tab shows an anon key and a service_role key. The template expects these two, not the newer publishable and secret pair on the first tab.

body.caption: The API Keys page. Click the Legacy anon, service_role API keys tab — the first tab shows the newer key pair, which the template does not use.

blocks.t: Copy the two Supabase values into the environment file
blocks.d: Copy the project URL and the anon key into their NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables, and the service_role key into its own variable, exactly as ENV.template names them.
blocks.expect: Three Supabase values are set and nothing has been pasted into a chat window.

body.t: The service role key is a master key
body.text: It ignores row level security and can read and write every row in the client's database. It must never sit in a variable whose name starts NEXT_PUBLIC_, never be committed, and never appear in a screenshot. If one is ever exposed, rotate it in Supabase the same day and tell the template owner.

blocks.t: Set the site's own address
blocks.d: Set NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL to the *.netlify.app address you recorded in task 2.3, with no trailing slash.
blocks.expect: The variable is set. Leaving it empty makes the site throw during the build rather than falling back to a default.

blocks.t: Get the Stripe test keys and a 100% coupon from the client
blocks.d: Through the account manager, ask the client for the test publishable key and test secret key from their Stripe account, or sandbox details, plus a 100% coupon for the WEB-005 test booking. [NEEDS INPUT: Q11 — whether Stripe is the client's own account and who swaps test for live]
blocks.expect: Two keys beginning pk_test_ and sk_test_, and a coupon code, in the client's 1Password vault.

body.label: Message for the account manager to forward
body.text: For <client>'s new site we need Stripe test access so we can prove the payment path without charging anyone: the test publishable key and test secret key from their Stripe dashboard (test mode), or sandbox login details, plus a 100% coupon code for one test booking. Please send them through 1Password, not email.

body.t: Test keys only
body.text: A key beginning sk_live_ never goes into .env.local. If the client sends live keys, put them in 1Password and stop; the live swap happens in WEB-005.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — Stripe's test-mode API keys screen, both values redacted before you send it. Ring the test-mode toggle.

blocks.t: Get the Resend API key
blocks.d: The Resend account is the client's. Invite hgmwebteam@gmail.com to it as a team member, then create the API key. [NEEDS INPUT: Q13, where the client's Resend login is kept]
blocks.expect: A Resend API key in .env.local under [NEEDS INPUT: the variable name in ENV.template].

body.caption: Resend → API keys → Create API key. Tokens hidden here.

blocks.t: Get the Meta pixel ID and access token
blocks.d: [NEEDS INPUT: Q19 — where the shared HGM conversions API token is kept, and whether the pixel ID is per client]
blocks.expect: Both values in .env.local.

blocks.t: Get the GoHighLevel Location ID and private integration token
blocks.d: In the client's GoHighLevel sub-account, click Settings at the bottom of the left side menu. Open Business Profile and copy the Location ID into GHL_LOCATION_ID. Then open Private Integrations, create a new integration named for the client's site (for example Awayframes Website), select only View Contacts and Edit Contacts as its scopes, and create it. Click Copy beside the token it shows and paste it into GHL_PIT.
blocks.expect: The Location ID matches the one on the client's record in hgmportal.com, the token begins pit-, and GHL_LOCATION_ID and GHL_PIT are both set in .env.local.

body.caption: GoHighLevel → Settings → Business Profile: the Location ID, with its copy button, top right.

body.t: Check which sub-account you are in
body.text: The sub-account's name is at the top of the left side menu. A token from the wrong sub-account sends this client's enquiries and bookings into another client's CRM, and nothing errors.

body.caption: Settings → Private Integrations, under Other settings. Each integration is named for what uses it, so the site's own is easy to find when its token is rotated.
The two scopes, View Contacts and Edit Contacts, and nothing else (2 of 180). The site only creates and updates contacts, so the token needs no more.
The token, shown once the integration is created. Click Copy and paste it straight into GHL_PIT. Token hidden here.

blocks.t: Get the booking platform's booking engine details
blocks.d: For Guesty: open Marketing + Sales → Distribution → Guesty Booking Engine and copy the booking engine API (BEAPI) URL. [NEEDS INPUT: Q17 — the variable it fills, and the Hostaway and Cloudbeds equivalents]
blocks.expect: The booking platform values are in .env.local.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — The booking platform's distribution screen where the booking engine URL is shown. Ring the URL field.

blocks.t: Put the variables on Netlify and rebuild
blocks.d: Ask Claude Code to set each variable from .env.local on the Netlify project, one at a time, then trigger a new deploy. If Claude cannot reach Netlify, add them by hand in Site configuration → Environment variables.
blocks.expect: The deploy succeeds and the netlify.app address serves the template's home page.

body.label: Claude prompt
body.note: needs the Netlify CLI logged in and linked
body.text: Using the Netlify CLI on the project linked to this repository, set each variable that has a value in .env.local and also appears in ENV.template, one at a time with netlify env:set. Skip NETLIFY_SITE_ID. Never use netlify env:import, never print a value, and list the variable names you set. If the CLI is not logged in or the site is not linked, stop and tell me.

body.t: Named variables only, never a bulk import
body.text: Importing .env.local whole uploads anything personal to your machine and arms every scheduled function the template ships. The prompt sets only names that are in ENV.template.

body.t: First run of the automated route
body.text: This replaces typing each variable in by hand. Check the list Claude prints against Netlify on the first build that uses it, and tell the Web & Content Specialist if anything was missed.

body.caption: Netlify → Project configuration → Environment variables → Add a variable, for the by-hand route.

blocks.t: Write the environment file back to 1Password
blocks.d: Save the current .env.local into the client's 1Password vault following HGM-SOP-WEB-001. Leave a key blank if the client has not supplied it yet; the blank is the record of what is still owed.
blocks.expect: Someone else could pick the build up tomorrow from 1Password alone, and WEB-005 task 1.3 finds the missing keys by their blank values.

body.t: Deferring a key is normal
body.text: Some keys are not needed until launch, and some clients are slow to supply them. Build without them and fill them in when they arrive — WEB-005 checks for blanks before anything goes live.

blocks.d: Gather the evidence the build gets checked against. Doing this properly is what makes phase 7 finite.

blocks.t: Create the folder structure
blocks.d: In the repository root, create Resources/ containing Page HTML/, Page PNG/, Design System/ and CSS/.
blocks.expect: Four empty folders, committed to the repository. They stay there — the evidence lives with the code.

body.caption: Resources/Page HTML and Resources/Page PNG on a finished build — one file per page of the original site, named for the page.

blocks.t: Save the HTML of every page on the original site
blocks.d: For each page in the original site's sitemap, save the rendered page source into Resources/Page HTML/, named for the page — Home.html, Listings.html, Checkout.html and so on.
blocks.expect: One HTML file per page. This is the copy that carries exact wording, field names and widget settings, which a screenshot cannot.

body.label: Claude prompt
body.note: fill in the live site's address
body.text:
Save the HTML of every page in <live-site>'s sitemap into
"Resources/Page HTML/", one file per page, named for the
page: Home.html, Listings.html, Checkout.html and so on.
Follow redirects. Make no other changes.

blocks.t: Capture every page as a full-page image
blocks.d: Capture each page of the original site top to bottom at 2× pixel density with a full-page capture extension — the team uses FireShot — and save it into Resources/Page PNG/, named for the page.
blocks.expect: One image per page, showing the whole page rather than the visible window.

body.t: Keep anything you attach to a prompt under 2000px wide
body.text: Claude handles an attached image poorly once it is wider than about 2000 pixels — it reads the picture but stops seeing the detail you are asking about. Capture at 2× for the archive, then resize the copy you attach so its longest edge is 2000 pixels or less.

blocks.t: Capture each section, the header and the footer separately
blocks.d: Capture every distinct section of the original — hero, search widget, listing grid, reviews, calls to action — plus the header and footer, at 2×, and save them into Resources/Design System/.
blocks.expect: A section-level library. Phase 7 attaches one of these per correction prompt, and a section capture is readable where a full-page capture is not.

blocks.t: Save the original site's stylesheets
blocks.d: Open the original site with the browser's Network panel filtered to CSS, reload, and save every stylesheet the page loads into Resources/CSS/ under its own filename.
blocks.expect: The site's real design values are now on disk as text. This is the exact source — a screenshot is an approximation of it.

body.t: Where the values actually live
body.text: On a WordPress and Elementor site the global kit stylesheet holds the whole palette as literal hex values, plus the type scale. On a modern build it is usually a block of CSS custom properties near the top of the main stylesheet. Either way it is machine-readable, which a capture is not.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — The browser's Network panel filtered to CSS on the original site, showing the stylesheet list. Ring the filter control.

blocks.t: Build the variables file from the stylesheets
blocks.d: In Claude Code, run the prompt below against Resources/CSS/. Save the result as Resources/VARIABLES.md.
blocks.expect: A Markdown file listing the site's colours, fonts, sizes, spacing, radii and breakpoints, each traceable to the declaration it came from, and each value you cannot trace listed as unresolved rather than filled in.

body.label: Build the variables file
body.text:
Read every stylesheet in Resources/CSS/ and write Resources/VARIABLES.md.

List the design tokens this site actually uses: colour ramps and semantic colours as hex, font families, font weights, the font-size scale, line heights, the spacing scale, border radii, shadows and breakpoints.

For every value, give the file and the declaration it came from. Where one role carries more than one value across the site, list them all and say which pages use which.

Do not infer a value you cannot point at in the CSS. List it under "Unresolved" instead, with what you were looking for.

body.t: Build it from the CSS, not from the captures
body.text: Asking for tokens from screenshots produces plausible hexes that are one or two shades out, and nobody catches it until the client does. The stylesheet carries the real numbers. Use the captures to check the file, not to write it.

blocks.t: Check the variables against the rendered page, then commit
blocks.d: Open three pages of the original in the browser. On each, use Inspect → Computed on the main heading, a paragraph of body text and the primary button, and compare the font, size, weight, colour and radius against VARIABLES.md. Correct the file where they differ, then commit the whole Resources/ folder.
blocks.expect: Every value you spot-checked matches what the browser actually renders, and everything the build will be judged against is pushed rather than sitting in one person's Downloads folder.

body.t: Where the file and the page disagree, the page wins
body.text: A stylesheet can carry declarations that something later overrides, so the computed value is the truth. Fix VARIABLES.md to match what renders, and note the override in the file so nobody re-introduces the dead value.

body.t: Capture the states a screenshot misses
body.text: While you are in the browser, capture the hover states, the open mobile menu, a form with a validation error showing, and any empty or sold-out state. Save them into Resources/Design System/. These are the details phase 7 is most likely to get wrong, because nothing in a static capture shows them.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — Devtools with Computed open on a heading, with font, size and colour visible.

blocks.d: Rework the template's plan for this client, read it yourself, and only then let anything be built.

blocks.t: Replace the template's placeholder client everywhere
blocks.d: Open PLAN.md and run find and replace across the file: the placeholder client name the template ships with, replaced by this client's name.
blocks.expect: No other client's name survives anywhere in PLAN.md. Search the file for the old name afterwards and confirm zero results.

body.t: This is the most common mistake in the whole build
body.text: A leftover client name in the plan gets built into the site — wrong phone number, wrong branding, wrong copy — and it is found weeks later by the client. Check the whole file, not just the headings.

blocks.t: Replace the property management system throughout
blocks.d: In the same file, replace every mention of the template's booking platform with the one this client uses. If the client's platform has no template, also run the prompt below before task 6.3.
blocks.expect: PLAN.md names one booking platform, it is the client's, and the booking sections are written for it.

body.label: Claude prompt
body.note: only when the platform has no template
body.text: This client is on <booking platform>, not <template's platform>. Its booking engine, API, listings, availability and reservation model are different. Research how <booking platform>'s API and booking engine work, then update plan.md so every section that touches booking, listings, availability or checkout is written for <booking platform>. List what you changed and anything you could not confirm.

blocks.t: Ask Claude to rewrite the plan against this project
blocks.d: In Claude Code, with the repository open, paste the prompt below with the four values filled in.
blocks.expect: PLAN.md now describes this client's build section by section, against this template, with the original site named as the target.

body.label: Rework the plan
body.note: Fill in the four angle-bracket values
body.text: Go through plan.md and update all the sections to reflect creating the website using the template which we defined at the top of the file. The website will be created and will be hosted on Netlify. The database will be Supabase, and the API will be <Guesty or Hostaway>. We are recreating the <live site URL> website, which was built using <WordPress/Elementor, or whatever the original was built in>, as a Next.js site. The plan should highlight in detail, with the same sections that are already in place, reproducing the website using the current plan. Update what is necessary.

body.t: Point the plan at the evidence
body.text: Add a line naming Resources/ as the reference set — the saved HTML, the captures and VARIABLES.md — so the plan is written against what is on disk rather than against the live site the model cannot see.

blocks.t: Read the plan yourself before executing it
blocks.d: Read PLAN.md end to end. Check the goal names the right site, the success conditions are ones you could test, every page in the original's sitemap appears, and any page deliberately left out is named as such.
blocks.expect: You could explain to Gillian what is being built and what is deliberately not. If you cannot, fix the plan before task 7.1.

body.caption: The top of a reworked PLAN.md — it names the template, the original site, the host, the database, the booking API, and the success conditions in priority order.

body.t: Nothing is built until the plan is right
body.text: Executing a wrong plan costs a day and a large share of the build's token budget, and the result looks finished enough that the error survives review. Reading the plan takes fifteen minutes.

blocks.text: Phase 7 — Build it and match it
blocks.d: Execute the plan, then close the gap between your copy and the original, section by section. This is where most of the elapsed time goes.

blocks.t: Execute the plan
blocks.d: In Claude Code, on a branch off main, run the prompt below and let it work through PLAN.md.
blocks.expect: The site runs on localhost with every page in the plan present. It will not yet match the original.

body.label: Execute the plan
body.text: Execute Plan.md, ensure there are no mistakes. Everything must be perfect.

blocks.t: Close the obvious gap against the original
blocks.d: Run the prompt below with the original site's URL. Use it once, to get from roughly right to close.
blocks.expect: Structure, page order and the large layout decisions now follow the original. Fine detail will not, and that is task 7.3's job.

body.label: Match the original
body.note: Drop the last line if Sentinel modes are not set up
body.text:
The website does not look exactly the same, create a loop and loop until everything looks exactly like <live site URL>. There can be no mistakes, everything must be perfect.

Use Sentinel Ultra and Sentinel.

body.t: A loop is a blunt instrument
body.text: Looping against a whole site gets you close and then stops improving, while spending tokens on every pass. Run it once, then switch to task 7.3. Looping a second time is the single easiest way to waste a day.

blocks.t: Correct the site section by section, in one pass
blocks.d: Open the original and your local site side by side. Write one prompt that names every section that is wrong, says what is wrong with each, and attaches the matching capture from Resources/Design System/ plus a capture of your version.
blocks.expect: Each section moves towards the original in one round rather than several. Re-capture your site and repeat until the list is empty.

body.label: A real correction pass
body.text:
1) Edit the listings page's Quick tour section to remove the gallery button on every image and just have each image link to the gallery.
2) Can we go three wide here, not four? It is too squished.
3) Wrong phone number — it should be the same phone number as the rest of the site.
4) Reduce the height of this pop-up card by shrinking the height of the image on the right and removing the large amount of spacing on the left between the form and the title and the bottom of the area. Snug the text up to near the bottom of the form if possible. Good UX/UI please.

body.t: One large prompt beats a loop
body.text: Addressing every section in a single well-written prompt has consistently produced better results than asking for a loop. Be specific about what is wrong; "make it match" produces a rewrite, and a rewrite breaks the sections that were already right.

body.caption: The Claude Code prompt box in VS Code — the attached capture sits above the prompt as a chip, and the file in context sits on the toolbar beside the model.

body.t: Resize before you attach
body.text: Attach nothing wider than 2000 pixels. An oversized capture is read as a picture rather than as evidence, and the correction comes back generic.

blocks.t: Build the form in GoHighLevel
blocks.d: Open the client's GoHighLevel sub-account, go to Sites → Forms, start from the HGM form template, and adjust the fields to match the form on the original site.
blocks.expect: A saved form in the client's own sub-account, with the same fields the original site asked for and no extras.

body.t: Check which sub-account you are in
body.text: A form built in the wrong sub-account sends one client's enquiries into another client's CRM, and nothing errors — the submission simply lands in the wrong place. Confirm the location before you build, and confirm the Location ID on the client's record in hgmportal.com matches the one you are working in.

body.t: Labels can differ
body.text: HGM's GoHighLevel is white-labelled, so a menu may not read exactly as it does in GoHighLevel's own documentation. Follow the equivalent item rather than looking for the literal words.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — GoHighLevel Sites → Forms with the HGM form template in the list. Ring the template row.

blocks.t: Copy the form's embed code
blocks.d: In the form builder, click Integrate form, choose Inline as the embed type, and copy the embed code.
blocks.expect: An iframe snippet on your clipboard, pointing at the form you just built.

body.t: Take the inline embed even for the pop-up
body.text: The inline embed drops into a container you control, which is what the site's own pop-up needs. GoHighLevel's own pop-up embed brings its own overlay and fights the one built in task 7.7.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — The GoHighLevel form builder with the integrate control visible, then the embed dialog with the inline layout selected. Ring the Integrate form control.

blocks.t: Place the forms on the site
blocks.d: Give Claude the embed code and say where each form goes — inline in a named page, or inside the pop-up.
blocks.expect: Each form renders in place, sized to its container, on desktop and on a phone.

body.t: The form is not ours to restyle
body.text: Fields, validation and where a submission lands are configured in GoHighLevel, inside the iframe. Everything built here is the container around the embed.

body.t: Submit one of each before you move on
body.text: Send a test submission through every form on the site and confirm it appears as a contact in the client's GoHighLevel sub-account. A form that renders and does not deliver looks identical to one that works.

blocks.t: Build the pop-up
blocks.d: Attach the pop-up captures from Resources/Design System/ and ask for the same design at every screen size, with the offer wording taken from the Asana task.
blocks.expect: One pop-up design, correct on a phone and on a desktop, showing the offer the client actually agreed.

body.label: Pop-up
body.note: Replace the offer with the one on the Asana task
body.text: Build the pop-up to match the attached design. Keep a similar design on all screen sizes but allow different content where the layout needs it. The offer is 10% off, not a fixed dollar amount.

body.t: Check the offer against the task, not the design file
body.text: Offer wording changes after a design is signed off more often than the design gets updated. A percentage and a dollar amount are not interchangeable, and the wrong one is a discount HGM has published on the client's behalf.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — The finished pop-up on a phone width and on a desktop width, side by side.

blocks.t: Agree the mobile menu before building it
blocks.d: The original site's mobile menu is rarely in the design and rarely worth copying. Post a capture of the original's mobile menu in the client websites space in Google Chat, propose what you intend to build, and get a reply before building it.
blocks.expect: A written decision from the designer or the account manager. Build that.

body.label: Post in the client websites space
body.text: <client> mobile menu — the original uses <describe it>. I am proposing <what you intend to build> instead, because <reason>. Shout before end of day if you would rather I copied the original exactly.

blocks.t: Add the motion
blocks.d: Ask for the site's animations in one pass, naming the motion skill so the result is consistent rather than improvised per section.
blocks.expect: Elements enter and transition consistently across every page, and nothing moves for a visitor who has reduced motion turned on.

body.label: Animations
body.text: Add an immersive experience by applying the appropriate animations to all the pages — for example elements fading in — using the /emil-design-eng skill.

body.t: Install the skill first
body.text: The /emil-design-eng command only works if the skill is installed in your Claude Code. Install it from [NEEDS INPUT: where the team gets the emil-design-eng skill] before you run the prompt.

blocks.t: Ask Claude to check the build works like the original
blocks.d: Run the prompt below. It checks function, not looks — including the parts you cannot see.
blocks.expect: A list of what works, what does not and what was fixed. Treat it as a first pass; task 7.11 is the check that counts.

body.label: Claude prompt
body.text: Compare this build with <live site URL> for function, not appearance. Check every page loads, every link and button goes where the original's does, every form submits, listings and their images load from Supabase and the booking platform, the search widget returns results, and nothing in the browser console errors. Fix what is broken, then list what you checked, what you fixed and anything you could not check.

blocks.t: Check it yourself: every page, every button
blocks.d: Open the build on localhost. Go to every page in the sitemap and click every link, button, menu and form. Try to break it. Write down anything that fails and give the list to Claude in one prompt, as in task 7.3.
blocks.expect: Every page opens, every control does something, and nothing on your list is still broken.

blocks.t: Walk the booking flow as a guest
blocks.d: Start at the search widget on the home page. Choose dates, guests and pets if the site asks, and search. On the stays page, check the widget shows what you chose. Open a property and check its listing page shows the same dates and guests, so the guest never chooses them twice.
blocks.expect: A guest can get from the home page to a property page with their dates intact. Stop there.

body.t: Stop at the property page
body.text: Prices, deposits, checkout, coupons and anything that creates a charge are not built or altered in this SOP. That work is done in the pre-launch SOP, in Claude Fable, against a test key. A mistake past this line charges a real person the wrong amount.

body.t: Image to be added
body.text: (image to be added) — The finished build's search widget with dates and guests filled in, and the property page it leads to.

blocks.t: Check the original site has not changed during the build
blocks.d: Run the prompt below against the original.
blocks.expect: Either nothing changed, or the changed pages are re-captured into Resources/ and rebuilt.

body.label: Claude prompt
body.text: Compare <live site URL> today with the captures in Resources/Page HTML and Resources/Page PNG. List every page whose content, layout or wording has changed since they were saved. Make no changes to the build.

blocks.d: Record what the build cost, get it reviewed by the team, and pass it to pre-launch.

blocks.t: Record what the build cost
blocks.d: In Claude Code, ask for the approximate token count for the work, convert it to Canadian dollars, and append a row to TOKENS.md.
blocks.expect: TOKENS.md has a row per session and a running total. Operations can see the real cost of a build rather than an estimate.

body.label: Token count
body.text: Give me the approximate tokens used from the start of this project to now, then convert those tokens to USD and then to CAD at today's rate. Append the result as a row in TOKENS.md with today's date.

body.t: Why this is worth the two minutes
body.text: The long-term aim is a defensible cost per build, and the input to that is a per-session figure recorded while the session is still in memory. Reconstructing it afterwards is guesswork.

blocks.t: Push the branch and open a pull request
blocks.d: Push your branch and open a pull request against main, following HGM-SOP-WEB-002 phase 5.
blocks.expect: Netlify builds a deploy preview and posts its link on the pull request.

blocks.t: Post the site for team review
blocks.d: Post the deploy preview link in the client websites space in Google Chat and ask the team to review it for mistakes and issues.
blocks.expect: The team has the link and a deadline. Work through what comes back, then merge the pull request so the netlify.app address carries it.

body.label: Post in the client websites space
body.text:
<client> rebuild is ready for a look: <deploy preview URL>

Original for comparison: <live site URL>

Looking for anything that does not match the original, on desktop and on a phone. Known gaps: <list them>. Comments by <date> please — it moves to pre-launch checks after that.

blocks.t: Send the site to the account manager
blocks.d: Once the team's comments are fixed and merged, post the netlify.app address in the client websites space for the account manager and ask them to review it before the client sees it.
blocks.expect: The account manager has the link and replies with changes or a go-ahead to send it to the client.

body.label: Post in the client websites space
body.text: @<account manager> <client>'s new site is ready for your review before it goes to the client: <netlify.app URL>. Original for comparison: <live site URL>. Reply here with anything to change, or a go-ahead to send it on.

blocks.t: Work through the client's revisions
blocks.d: The account manager sends the site to the client. Make each change they ask for through the HGM-SOP-WEB-002 branch-and-preview path, until the client has no open comments.
blocks.expect: Every revision is merged and the netlify.app address shows it.

blocks.t: Confirm the client has approved, then hand on
blocks.d: When the account manager confirms the client has approved the site, post in the client websites space that the build is moving to pre-launch, with the netlify.app address and the TOKENS.md total.
blocks.expect: The build is approved and somebody else could take it to launch without asking you a question. Continue in WEB-005.

body.label: Post in the client websites space
body.text: <client> is approved by the client and moving to pre-launch (WEB-005): <netlify.app URL>. Build cost so far: <TOKENS.md total>.

body.t: No approval, no pre-launch
body.text: WEB-005 starts only after the client has approved the site and every revision is done.

items.t: A page in the original is deliberately not being rebuilt
items.d: Name it in PLAN.md as out of scope and say what happens to its URL instead — usually a redirect. An unlisted omission is indistinguishable from a page somebody forgot.

blocks.t: If you are stuck
blocks.text: Ask Claude first, with the error and the task number. If the template itself is wrong, stale or missing a file, tell Leshan Patterson, template owner, in the client websites space in Google Chat. If the build is going to take longer than the request assumed, tell Gillian, Operations Manager, in Google Chat in phase 5 — when you can see how big the original is — not in phase 7.

blocks.label: Final checklist before you hand the build on

items: Every page in the original site's sitemap exists on the build, or is named in PLAN.md as out of scope with its redirect.
No other client's name appears anywhere in the repository — search the whole project, not just PLAN.md.
Resources/ is committed and holds the saved HTML, the page captures, the section captures, the stylesheets and VARIABLES.md.
Every colour, font and size on the build traces to a value in VARIABLES.md, and nothing in that file is still marked unresolved.
.env.local is not committed, and its current contents are saved in the client's 1Password vault.
Every variable on Netlify matches the one in .env.local, and the production deploy succeeds.
A test submission from every form has appeared as a contact in the client's GoHighLevel sub-account.
The HGM web team account is a member of the client's Netlify team, and the client is still its Owner.
The booking flow runs from the home page search to a property page with dates carried through.
Nothing in the pricing or payment path has been altered.
The site is on its netlify.app address and no DNS record has been changed.
TOKENS.md has a row for every session and a total.
.env.local is saved to the client's 1Password vault, with a blank for every key still owed.
Claude's function check (7.10) and your own every-page check (7.11) are done, and nothing on either list is open.
The team, then the account manager, then the client have reviewed the site; every revision is merged and the client has approved.
blocks.prompt: Check this project against the final checklist below. For each line, say pass or fail and give the evidence — a command output, a file path or a URL. Make no changes.

items.d: HGM-SOP-WEB-005 — SEO and GEO, accessibility to WCAG 2.2 AA, the Lighthouse loop, BrowserStack, legal pages, the pixels, the Stripe and webhook work, the test booking and the DNS cutover. Starts once the client has approved the site.
HGM-SOP-WEB-003 — Google Analytics 4, Search Console, Hotjar, the structured-data check and the ownership map at handover. Starts the day the site is live.

blocks.text: This SOP is the middle of three. It ends where the site is complete on its temporary address; the next document takes it to launch, and the one after that picks it up once it is live.

blocks.t: The build is not finished when the site looks right
blocks.text: A site that matches the original and has never been through the pre-launch checks is not ready for a client, let alone a domain. Task 8.6 hands it on; do not treat a merged pull request as the end of the job.
